$comment: DIG URN parse conformance table — the AUTHORITY for agreement between the DIG URN parsers.
The parsed resourceKey and salt feed retrieval-key and decryption-key derivation, so two
implementations that parse one URN differently derive different keys and read different bytes.
Agreement therefore has to be verifiable, not asserted in a comment: run your parser against
Each case is { urn, expect } where expect is either the parsed parts or { invalid: true }.
Shipped inside the npm package, so a consumer reads it from
Salt-parameter rules this table encodes, all normative (SPEC.md 7.1). ONE boundary rule governs
both decisions: a 'salt=' counts only at the start of the query or right after an '&', and the
query is split off ONLY when such a boundary 'salt=' is present (a '?' is legal in a resource key,
so a broader split truncates working keys). Values are NOT percent-decoded; the parameter name is
case-sensitive; the first boundary occurrence with a hex value wins; an empty or valueless salt is
null; and the value is the leading hex run.

cases.name: canonical rootless form
root-pinned form; the root is lowercased, the key is not
salt in final position
salt NON-final, with a trailing parameter — the salt is still a query parameter, and the rest of the query is not part of the key (#2518)
salt after another parameter
salt followed by a fragment; the fragment is part of the query tail and discarded with it
a store key containing a literal '#' — NOT a fragment. Only the query is stripped, so this working key keeps working
a '#'-containing key WITH a salt: the '#' survives, the query does not
a non-hex salt value is not a salt
an empty resource key is not a URN; the default-view resolution happens in key derivation, not here
a store id that is not 64 hex is not a URN
not a URN at all
a resource key containing a literal '?' and NO salt is preserved VERBATIM — it is a real working key, so the query is split off only when the query segment contains 'salt=' (#2518 reviewer finding 1)
the same key WITH a salt: the query does carry a salt, so it is split off
percent-encoding is NOT decoded: '%61%61' is not a hex salt value, so there is no salt (a URLSearchParams-based sibling would read 'aa' here and derive a DIFFERENT key)
an EMPTY salt value is not a salt (a sibling reading '' would derive a different key)
a valueless 'salt' (no '=') is not a salt parameter at all, so the string is not even treated as a query
FIRST occurrence wins on a duplicated parameter
the parameter name is CASE-SENSITIVE: '?SALT=' is not a salt, and the string is left verbatim
the case-sensitivity rule in MIXED case: '?SaLt=' is not a salt parameter either, so it is neither read as a salt nor treated as a query marker
case sensitivity in NON-FINAL position: an uppercase name after another parameter is still not a salt, and the whole tail stays in the key

case sensitivity changing the SPLIT decision: a '?SALT=' tail cannot qualify a '?' as the start of a query, so a real '?'-containing key survives whole (a case-insensitive sibling truncates it to 'report?year=2024.csv')

case sensitivity changing the SALT VALUE: an uppercase name preceding a real lowercase one is skipped, so the salt is 'bbbb' — a case-insensitive sibling reads 'aaaa' and derives a decryption key that cannot read the content
a key whose FIRST character is '#': stripping the '#' as a fragment leaves an empty key, so a '#'-stripping sibling rejects a URN that is valid
'#' and '?' in ONE key with no salt anywhere: neither is a delimiter here, so the whole remainder is the key

the leading-hex-run rule in NON-FINAL position: the value ends at the first non-hex character and the parameter continues, so the salt is 'ff' — a parser requiring the whole value to be hex reads no salt at all here

'salt=' inside ANOTHER parameter's value is not a salt parameter AND not a query marker: it must sit at a parameter boundary, so the key is preserved VERBATIM (a broader split predicate truncates a key carrying no secret at all)
the PROPERTY behind the row above, on a key that merely contains the substring 'salt=' with no parameter anywhere: a query carrying no boundary salt leaves the resource key verbatim
the first boundary occurrence carrying a HEX value wins: an earlier empty one is skipped, so this is 'bbbb' (a parser that stops at the first occurrence unconditionally derives a different key)
the value is the LEADING HEX RUN, ending at the first non-hex character — a parser requiring the whole value to be hex would read null here and derive a different key

a '?'-containing key WITH a salt appended after a SECOND '?' — the natural way to salt such a key, and the grammar's own form. Every '?' is a split candidate, so a parser that only ever considers the FIRST one leaves the secret inside resourceKey (#2518) and derives a different key

when more than one '?' carries a salt parameter the FIRST qualifying one wins, because it strips the most — splitting at the last would leave the earlier 'salt=aa' inside the resource key, which is the leak direction

a chosen query tail carrying a further '?'-borne salt=: once a '?' has been judged to START the query, every later '?' inside it is a separator, so the salt is read there too. Honouring only '&' inside the tail derived NO salt for this URN — silently undecryptable — while SPEC's boundary definition names it
a URN whose resource key is ONLY a salt query has an empty key once the query is removed, and an empty resource key is not a URN

two DISTINCT usable salts: the FIRST boundary occurrence wins even when a '?' introduced it and an '&' introduced the later one (published 0.6.3 read the LATER value's shape as no salt at all, so no working read changes)
